summary: Robert Braden explains that UCLA's computing center did not plan to be a post-office host and only wanted mail for its own staff, which it would print and deliver by courier. He also praises the simple Tenex SNDMSG command, which uses the FTP MAIL command to deliver messages without logging in.

plainLanguage.summary: A computer center said it only wanted letters for its own people, would print them out for delivery, and liked a simple mail program.

subtitle: Robert Braden explains UCLA's mail policy and proposes extensions to FTP mail.

tldr.problem: Mail protocols under development assumed all hosts would act as full post offices, but UCLA Computing Center wanted to receive mail only for its own staff, which would be printed and delivered by courier rather than stored online.
tldr.mechanism: Braden praises the simple SNDMSG command, which uses FTP's MAIL command to deliver messages without requiring a login. He proposes extensions to MAIL and MLFL (Mail File) commands in FTP to allow UCLA to serve as a delivery station, with syntax for specifying document vs. message, copies, and output bin.
tldr.outcome: The proposal was adopted, extending FTP with mail parameters for proper charging and delivery handling. The simple SNDMSG approach showed that mail services did not need to be complex to be useful.

today: RFC 498 documents early network mail practices from 1973. The concepts of mail delivery without login and of extending protocols with optional parameters remain relevant in modern email infrastructure.

sections.title: UCLA's Mail Policy
sections.content: RFC 498 is Robert Braden's statement on UCLA Computing Center's approach to network mail. UCLA does not plan to be a full mail post office hosting accounts for other sites. Instead, it receives mail only for its own staff, prints all messages immediately, and delivers them by courier or secretary within a few hours. This policy is designed to keep administration simple and support the center's administrative and user support staff who do not regularly use online terminals.
sections.plainLanguage: The computer center said they would only accept letters for their own people, print them on paper, and have someone deliver them in person.

sections.title: The SNDMSG Command
sections.content: Braden praises the TENEX SNDMSG command as exceptionally useful despite its simplicity. SNDMSG uses FTP's MAIL command to send messages without requiring the sender to log into FTP. To send a message to a UCLA user, one types SNDMSG to "name@CCN", which connects to UCLA's FTP, issues a MAIL command with the recipient's name, sends the message, and disconnects. This elegant approach does not demand a password or authentication, making it accessible to any network user. UCLA accepts any name format and prints upper-case copies immediately for distribution.
sections.plainLanguage: A simple command lets anyone on the network send a message to anyone at UCLA without passwords or complicated steps.

sections.title: Proposed FTP Mail Extensions
sections.content: Braden proposes extending FTP's MAIL and MLFL commands with optional parameters in the user-name field, separated by semicolons. Parameters include ;MESSAGE (print immediately in uppercase, the default), ;DOCUMENT (queue for overnight printing in mixed case), ;COPIES (future feature for multiple copies), and ;BIN (specify the output bin, defaulting to bin 9906 for ARPA mail). Each message is time-and-date-stamped for tracking. These extensions allow UCLA to provide proper accounting, handle different message types appropriately, and manage output routing.
sections.plainLanguage: The mail commands were extended with special instructions like whether to print right away or save for later, how many copies to make, and where to put the output.
